title: We Need 'Curriculum Transparency,' But Not the Kind Some State Bills Would Require
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Wexler responds to state bills requiring schools to post instructional materials online, arguing that curriculum transparency is worth having but not for the politicized reasons driving the legislation. Most schools have not been transparent because of a longstanding assumption that curriculum is unimportant and that good teachers build their own, leaving teachers to spend about twelve hours a week hunting for mostly mediocre materials. She argues genuine transparency would help parents find schools teaching reading effectively through phonics and content-rich curricula and let them reinforce classroom learning. Framing it as a tool to challenge divisive texts risks pushing schools toward content-free skills curricula, which would hurt children with the least outside access to academic knowledge.
points: Most states, districts and even principals do not know what materials teachers use, so posting a curriculum online is harder than advocates suggest.
The tradition that teachers should write their own curriculum costs about twelve hours a week and yields mostly mediocre materials.
Real transparency would let parents judge reading instruction and extend classroom topics at home.
Politicizing transparency may drive schools toward contentless skills curricula, harming the children who most need academic knowledge.
quotes: But in fact, most schools and districts—good or otherwise—have not been particularly transparent about curriculum, especially at the elementary level. That’s not because they’ve been trying to hide anything. The reasons are more complex.

As researcher Morgan Polikoff has found, most state education officials are clueless about what materials are actually being used in school districts. Local district officials often don’t know what materials are being used in school buildings. Even principals may be unclear about what teachers are using in the classroom down the hall.

How could this be? There’s a longstanding assumption on the part of American educators that curriculum just isn’t that important. In many schools, teachers have traditionally created the curriculum themselves, using state academic standards as a guide. Even when there is an officially adopted curriculum, many teachers have learned during their training that a “good” teacher doesn’t follow it closely.

The result is that teachers spend huge amounts of time either creating classroom materials or searching for them online—an average of about 12 hours a week, according to one study. Virtually all teachers report using Google to plan their lessons, and many use websites like Pinterest or Teachers Pay Teachers. Unfortunately, another study has found that most of the materials available online are “mediocre” or “probably not worth using.

School websites and district listings provide all kinds of information—about demographics, test scores, extracurricular activities. But it’s rare to find anything specific about a school’s curriculum.
Politicizing the issue of curriculum transparency in this way is both cynical and dangerous. Research has shown that high-quality curriculum can provide a powerful boost to students’ learning.

If curriculum transparency is reduced to a vehicle for challenges to supposedly offensive or divisive texts, schools may shy away from including any content in their curricula. They’ll stick with or return to an ELA curriculum that consists of the usual round of “comprehension skills” and doesn’t specify any content whatsoever.
